item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Palestinian students and staff sue Columbia University over discrimination
item.description:
Palestinian students and staff sue Columbia University over discrimination

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 08/12/2026 - 17:30
Lawsuit accuses the university of surveillance, biased disciplinary proceedings and failing to protect Palestinians
A pro-Israel supporter (right) confronts people at a vigil and protest for Palestine outside of Columbia University in New York City, on 7 October 2025 (Adam Gray/Getty Images/AFP)
Off

A group of current and former Palestinian students and staff have sued Columbia University, accusing the Ivy League school of discriminating against Palestinians and targeting pro-Palestinian activism on campus.

The lawsuit, filed in New York State Supreme Court this week, alleges that Columbia subjected Palestinian students, faculty and staff to unequal treatment following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023 and the ensuing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza perpetrated by Israel.

According to the complaint, Columbia "actively participated in and amplified" what the plaintiffs describe as racially, ethnically and politically motivated targeting of Palestinians.

Mahmoud Khalil, the Palestinian activist and former Columbia graduate student, also highlighted the lawsuit on X, saying Palestinian students were suing the university over alleged discrimination in its response to the protests in support of Palestinians and Gaza.

Proud of my fellow Palestinian students and faculty suing @Columbia for its abhorrent discrimination against Palestinians and anyone who stands with us.

Columbia chose to reward those who attacked us and to silence its own community while Israel bombed and starved Gaza. We will… https://t.co/XPtRQusYFJ

— Mahmoud Khalil | محمود خليل (@mahmoudkhalel) August 10, 2026

The plaintiffs say the university failed to adequately protect Palestinian members of its community from harassment while subjecting pro-Palestinian activists to "unfair and biased disciplinary hearings".

Columbia declined to comment on the pending litigation, according to local media, and did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Among the allegations is that Columbia hired private investigators to surveil students involved in the March 2024 "Resistance 101" event. Six students were subsequently suspended and evicted from university housing, according to the lawsuit.

The filing also accuses the university of failing to adequately respond to alleged physical attacks against Palestinians, including incidents in which students had their keffiyehs forcibly removed and the January 2024 spraying of a foul-smelling substance at a pro-Palestinian demonstration.

The lawsuit also challenges Columbia's decision to call New York City police onto campus to dismantle pro-Palestinian protest encampments and arrest demonstrators in 2024.

The plaintiffs include lecturer and former anthropology student Hadeel Assali; former lecturer Bahia Munem; PhD student Mahdi Sabbagh; 2025 graduate and former student organiser Maryam Alwan; and Layla Saliba, who graduated from Columbia's School of Social Work in 2025.

Saliba was among Palestinian students who had previously accused Columbia of discrimination in a federal civil rights complaint filed in 2024. At the time, she said Palestinian students were being treated poorly and called on the university to recognise anti-Palestinian racism.

Columbia under pressure

The case comes after years of controversy over Columbia's handling of protests against Israel's war on Gaza.

Columbia University student workers’ union withdraws Israel divestment demand
Read More »

In July 2025, Columbia reached a deal with the Trump administration to resolve federal investigations into alleged violations of anti-discrimination law and restore federal research funding that had been frozen by the government.

Under the agreement, the university agreed to pay $200m to the US government and another $21m to settle Equal Employment Opportunity Commission investigations concerning allegations of antisemitism against Jewish employees. Columbia did not admit wrongdoing or agree with the government's conclusion that it had violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act.

The university also settled a separate lawsuit brought by Jewish plaintiffs in February 2026 alleging that Columbia had failed to protect Jewish and Israeli students from antisemitism.

Palestinian activists and free-speech groups, meanwhile, have repeatedly accused Columbia of disproportionately punishing opposition to Israel. Reuters reported that students have faced arrests, suspensions, expulsions and degree revocations during the university's crackdown on pro-Palestinian protests.

The new lawsuit seeks monetary damages under New York City's Human Rights Law, which prohibits discrimination and harassment on grounds including race and national origin.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] New oral history project eulogises slain Palestinian journalists via friends' voice notes
item.description:
New oral history project eulogises slain Palestinian journalists via friends' voice notes

Submitted by MEE staff on Tue, 08/11/2026 - 16:56
The website's launch comes on the first anniversary of Israel's killing of Al Jazeera journalist Anas al-Sharif
A protester holds a photo of slain Al Jazeera journalist Anas al-Sharif, as part of the 'March for Humanity' for Gaza in New York City, on 16 August 2025 (Stephanie Keith/Getty Images via AFP)
Off

When Anas al-Sharif was killed in Gaza by an Israeli air strike one year ago, the Reuters news agency ran the headline, "Israel kills Al Jazeera journalist it says was Hamas leader". 

In 2024, at the height of Israel's genocide in Gaza, Anas had helped Reuters win a Pulitzer Prize for breaking news photography.

But the outlet chose to remember the 28-year-old within the scope of Israel's unproven narrative about him - as many other news organisations have done to more than 200 Palestinian journalists killed in Gaza since 2023.

As of Wednesday, a new project called The Living Record is looking to rectify that by telling the stories of slain Palestinian journalists through the eyes and experiences of their colleagues on the ground.

The oral history site launched with eulogies for 50 journalists, with dozens more to come later in the year.

"This project is seriously - and at a mammoth scale - a record of failure," a member of the New York War Crimes editorial collective, which was initiated by the group Writers Against The War On Gaza (Wawog), told Middle East Eye on the condition that they not be named. 

"[This is] a record of failure of mainstream media, of western media, of international institutions to protect individuals [as governed] by international law." 

Wawog is behind The Living Record. 

"What this project does is it asks you to listen to these people speaking to you as if they were your friend, and so that was one of the really big prompts of the project itself," MEE was told.

"Often when we spoke to these [Palestinian] journalists, there's a tendency for them to speak in a very formal register because they're accustomed to that being the only way that people would be willing to listen, whether on a live broadcast or in a formal interview where they're anticipating a critique or a challenge -  that they must present themselves as sort of indefatigable, impossible to move."

"We didn't want that." 

The result is profound.

The voice notes on the site range from journalists who sound broken but steadfast as they recount the relatable, daily habits of their colleagues, to others who speak directly to their slain friends, as if we, the audience, are listening in on a private conversation. 

Who is a journalist?

Many have resigned themselves to becoming "martyrs" at any moment.

That's because, according to the Palestinian Journalists Syndicate, at least 270 Palestinian media workers have been killed by Israel in Gaza.

The Committee to Protect Journalists, however, has a significantly lower count.

The mainstream media within the US and Canada have largely defaulted to CPJ for the figures, especially as most choose not to source local organisations or the Palestinian health ministry.

In June, CPJ came under fire when it announced it was "conducting a full review of its database of journalists killed during the Israel-Gaza War after militant groups Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad published obituaries identifying as combatants individuals previously listed by CPJ as journalists".

As a result, 20 Palestinian journalists were removed from CPJ's count, which now stands at 209 dead. The full review will be completed in the weeks to come, the group said.  

'This project is seriously - and at a mammoth scale - a record of failure'

- Member of Writers Against The War On Gaza

In its emailed statement to MEE at the time, CPJ said it "has not changed its longstanding methodology, which applies to all conflict zones around the world", nor has it "changed the way it classifies journalists".

But journalism itself is a "porous" industry, the Wawog member told MEE, especially in the so-called creator economy where thousands of journalists globally are leaving legacy outlets to go independent. 

"What you find with this project is that these are what we would call maybe 'traditional journalists', but we ask them to define themselves. In that sense, there is really no figure that we're trying to reach, but the archive is ongoing, and the expansion will go beyond just Gaza, and likely into south Lebanon." 

Wawog, a group made up of writers and creatives, emerged in the weeks following Israel's bombardment of Gaza after the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on 7 October 2023.

The group has routinely held protests outside, and at times in the lobby of, the New York Times building in the borough of Manhattan.

Wawog calls out what it sees as the hypocrisies of the New York Times in its own publication called "The New York War Crimes". 

Media analysts and human rights groups have repeatedly accused mainstream media of contributing to both the erasure and distortion of Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

Several observers have argued that the reporting on what the United Nations and holocaust scholars have called a genocide, as well as the student movement for Palestine in the US, has not merely been inaccurate but has ventured close to journalistic malpractice. 

Anas al-Sharif

Israeli forces assassinated two of Gaza's leading journalists and their colleagues late on Sunday, 10 August 2025, just hours after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected international condemnation over his plan to occupy the Palestinian enclave.

The Al Jazeera Media Network said in a statement that its correspondents Anas and Mohammed Qreiqeh, along with three other colleagues, were deliberately killed when Israeli forces struck their tent outside al-Shifa hospital in Gaza City.

Qreiqeh contributed to several publications, including Middle East Eye, before he began working at Al Jazeera. 

How six months in Israeli jail changed this Palestinian journalist’s life forever 
Read More »

Anas, a father of two, had been stationed outside the hospital's main gate along with cameramen and photojournalists Ibrahim Zaher, Mohammed Noufal and Mosaab al-Sharif when their tent was attacked.

Shortly before his killing, Anas had posted a video on X showing what he called Israel's "intense" missile strikes on the eastern and southern parts of Gaza City. His final video captured the deafening booms of the attacks near where he was.

Later, the Israeli military claimed, without providing any evidence, that it killed Anas because he "served as the head of a terrorist cell in the Hamas terrorist organisation".

Since Israel launched its war on the enclave in October 2023, it has routinely accused Palestinian journalists in Gaza of being Hamas members, as part of what rights groups say is an effort to discredit their reporting of Israeli abuses.

Four months before he was killed, Anas prepared a message to be posted on his social media accounts in the event of his death. 

"I have lived through pain in all its details, tasted suffering and loss many times, yet I never once hesitated to convey the truth as it is, without distortion or falsification - so that Allah may bear witness against those who stayed silent, those who accepted our killing, those who choked our breath, and whose hearts were unmoved by the scattered remains of our children and women," he wrote.

"I entrust you with Palestine - the jewel in the crown of the Muslim world, the heartbeat of every free person in this world," he added. 

"I entrust you with its people, with its wronged and innocent children who never had the time to dream or live in safety and peace. Their pure bodies were crushed under thousands of tons of Israeli bombs and missiles, torn apart and scattered across the walls."

Sharif pleaded: "I urge you not to let chains silence you."

The shortlist emerged from US-mediated talks in Rome last week, the latest round of negotiations between Israel and Lebanon on implementing a June agreement that ties Israel's phased withdrawal from Lebanon to the disarmament of Hezbollah.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi said that the country will be free of any foreign military presence on its soil and that weapons will be solely under state control by 1 October.

During a meeting with US Central Command Commander Charles Brad Cooper, Zaidi “affirmed the commitment to the agreed-upon timelines”, under which the international coalition’s military mission in Iraq and the withdrawal of its forces will be completed by 30 September, according to a statement published by his office.

1 October will therefore “mark a new day in the history of the Iraqi state”, as the country will be “free of any foreign military presence” and responsible for ensuring its own security and stability, the statement continued.

Zaidi added that weapons will henceforth be held only by state institutions, which will strengthen “the state’s authority and sovereignty, and guarantee security and stability”.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Pentagon tells Congress US killed 153 civilians in Yemen air strikes
item.description:
Pentagon tells Congress US killed 153 civilians in Yemen air strikes

Submitted by MEE staff on Wed, 08/12/2026 - 19:33
The Houthis have resumed attacks on vessels in the Red Sea despite enduring hundreds of US air strikes
A Yemeni man who was injured in US air strikes receives treatment at Al-Jumhuri Hospital in Yemen's Houthi-held capital Sanaa, on 8 May 2025 (Mohammed Huwais/AFP)
Off

The US killed and wounded hundreds of Yemeni civilians during its attacks on the country last year, according to an internal US Department of War assessment shared with Congress.

The US killed 153 civilians and wounded 243, the Pentagon said in a 12-page report that was sent to the Senate Armed Services Committee on Monday and reported by several news sites in the US.

US President Donald Trump ordered the American military to begin bombing the Houthis in March 2025. The attacks came in response to Houthi strikes on vessels in the Red Sea, which the group said were in solidarity with besieged Palestinians in Gaza.

The report detailed several specific strikes that the Pentagon said “more likely than not” caused civilian deaths and injuries. The report noted a 6 April attack on Sanaa that killed five civilians and wounded 25 others.

The report also noted a 17 April US attack on Hodeidah that killed at least 80 civilians. In a June report, Human Rights Watch said the attack should be investigated as a war crime.

“The US government’s decision to strike Ras Issa Port, a critical entry point for aid in Yemen, while hundreds of workers were present demonstrates a callous disregard for civilians’ lives,” Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen and Bahrain researcher at Human Rights Watch, said.

A US air strike at the end of April also killed at least 68 African migrants in Yemen's northwestern province of Saada.

Saudi Arabia mulls military escalation in response to Houthi threats
Read More »

The report said that there are 15 incidents related to the air strikes that are under review by the Pentagon.

The Trump administration’s decision to attack the Houthis was overshadowed initially by the SignalGate leaks.

Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg was mistakenly added to a Signal group chat that included 19 senior US officials planning the military campaign, including Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, United Nations ambassador Mike Waltz, and envoy Steve Witkoff.

The chat offered a rare window into the Trump administration’s planning for the attacks and deliberations, which focused on complaining about Europe and Egypt not remunerating Washington.

The Houthis endured more than 1,000 US strikes. The campaign was called off in May 2025 before Trump visited the Gulf. Middle East Eye revealed that Saudi Arabia pressed the US to end the attacks before the president’s visit.

Several regional officials told MEE that the US’s campaign did serious damage to the Houthis' military arsenal, but the impact proved fleeting. The group has resumed its attacks in the Red Sea and expanded them to target Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure.

item.description:
Saudi Arabia opposed Egypt's inclusion in Mecca agreement, sources say

Saudi Arabia opposed Egypt joining the security pact signed with Turkey and Pakistan last week, despite Ankara's push for Cairo to be included, three Saudi sources familiar with the discussions told Middle East Eye.

One of the sources, a former senior adviser to the Saudi monarchy, said Riyadh did not want Egypt to join the agreement "at least for now".

All three sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the issue, said the Saudi position was driven by a growing frustration with President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi's government and a belief in Riyadh that Egypt no longer offered the strategic or military value it once did.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which was signed in the Holy Muslim city of Mecca on Friday, commits Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan to regard an armed attack against any one of the three countries as an attack against all three.

According to the sources, the Saudi decision to oppose Egypt's entry was due to simmering tensions between Riyadh and Cairo.

Saudi Arabia reportedly blocked Egypt from joining its defence pact with Turkey and Pakistan, despite Ankara pushing for Cairo's inclusion. Saudi sources told MEE the decision reflects growing tensions with Egypt and doubts over its strategic value. pic.twitter.com/fX2Fg5iQSy

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Surrogate mother who fled to Texas gives birth to baby with severe heart defect
item.description:
McKenna West initially agreed to an abortion after diagnosis, but then fled to state where abortion is illegal and broke contact with biological parents, attorney alleges

A surrogate mother who traveled to Texas, where abortion is illegal, claiming she was pressured to end the pregnancy after the discovery of a severe heart defect, gave birth on Wednesday to a baby boy.

The child’s biological parents, Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed of California, confirmed the birth through their lawyer, while denying they forced McKenna West, who is from Alaska, to undergo an abortion, the Texas Tribune reported.

Telstra has paid its chief executive, Vicki Brady, $6.8m for the year ending in June, after docking 20% of her bonus in response to the network’s nationwide outage in July.

The company reported financial results on Thursday. Its board met on Monday and decided to cut Brady’s bonus by $607,000 – but she still took home a $700,000 pay rise as she was awarded a total of $6.1m the year before.

Iran's Araghchi slams France for 'hypocrisy' over human rights

Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi criticised France and other countries for what he described as "hypocrisy" when it comes to human rights and international law amid continued support for Israel.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Victims of road crime feel ‘forgotten by system’, official review finds
item.description:
Many of those affected in England and Wales think offences are not treated with the seriousness they deserve, says commissioner

Bereaved families or seriously injured victims of road crime feel “forgotten by the system” with offences not treated with the seriousness they deserve, an official review has found.

The victims’ commissioner for England and Wales found that many of the thousands afflicted each year by criminal driving felt that “the harm they had suffered mattered less” than that from other serious crimes.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] India fuels worldwide jump in planned coal production
item.description:
Rise in new mine proposals, mainly in states of Odisha and Jharkhand, comes despite plateau in global demand

Enough new coalmining projects were proposed last year to increase global supplies by 2.5bn tonnes a year, an increase of 11% from the year before, even as demand for coal plateaus, according to a new report.

Global Energy Monitor, an NGO, found that India ignited a rise in new coalmine proposals in 2025 despite a global slowdown in the number of mine openings because of falling demand for the fossil fuel.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] CIA had ‘low confidence’ in Israel's claims of Iranian threat to Trump: Report
item.description:
CIA had ‘low confidence’ in Israel's claims of Iranian threat to Trump: Report

US intelligence officials were sceptical of an alleged Iranian assassination threat against Donald Trump that was relayed by Israel, sources told The Washington Post. 

The threat was relayed by the Israeli government to the CIA, but analysts had doubts about the credibility of the information and conveyed their thoughts to the Trump administration, one official indicated. 

Another official described the reports of threats against the US president's life as "Israeli-derived, not U.S.-generated, and viewed as low confidence".

Earlier, The Washington Post broke the story that Trump secretly left Ankara on the military aircraft amid an alleged Iranian assassination threat.

The latest report follows confirmation of Trump secretly leaving Turkey on a military aircraft, instead of an Air Force One jumbo jet he was seen on television boarding.
